attribution.note: These are Marcus's own words in a co-authored post he published and endorses. He makes the comparison about the first author's child himself; he is not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the scope to one named child, the task (five-digit multiplication) and the unnamed LLM comparator. It is a present-tense observation.

contract.note: The speaker named a specific child, so asking for a documented comparison with that child is fair. The ordinary reading of five-digit multiplication and of accuracy is reasonable. Generic benchmarks rightly cannot settle it.

evidence.note: A May 2023 preprint on transformer failures at multi-digit multiplication. It is dated before the post and relevant on the model side, but it does not test the named child, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: The claim turns on how one particular child performed against an LLM. The packet has no inspectable record of the child, no matched problem set and no identified model. The model-side research is context only. The available evidence does not settle the comparison.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post. He applies a definition he wrote earlier and endorses.

semantics.note: The proposition correctly unpacks 'this' as the flexible, general, human-comparable resourcefulness and reliability standard, and keeps the stress on reliability.

contract.note: The plain reading (no current system meets the combined human-comparable standard) is ordinary and fair. It rightly allows for human error. The result depends on how the threshold and the human baseline are interpreted.

evidence.note: A June 2023 version, dated before the post. It documents failures on trivial compositional problems, which supports the reliability concern, but it has no human baseline and covers only LLMs.
AgentBench, August 2023. It shows real agent capability alongside instruction-following failures. There is no human comparison, so it qualifies the claim but does not settle it.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows LLMs failing on simple multi-step tasks and also showing notable agent capabilities. It never measures them against a common human baseline across general tasks, which the support and contradiction conditions require. The broader scope ('machines') is also untested. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own argument. He cites Kambhampati's findings to back his premise, but he endorses the inference himself.

semantics.note: The proposition drops the hedge that true AGI 'might' revolve around planning, which is what links the premises to the conclusion. The conclusion itself is an evidential 'strongly suggesting', not a firm claim. This is a hedged causal inference, not an observation.

contract.note: The contract applies a plain reading to hedged language. Its support condition asks for proof that a necessary capability is missing, which is more than the speaker's 'strongly suggesting' commits him to.

evidence.note: Kambhampati group, May 2023: GPT-4 produced valid Blocksworld plans only about a third of the time. This supports the planning-weakness premise only, not the missing-invention inference.
May 2023 study of snowballing hallucinations. Models can recognise many of their own mistakes, so hallucination alone does not show which capability is missing.
October 2023 Othello-GPT preprint, dated before the post. It finds a world representation in a narrow game model, which is not evidence of general LLM world-model maintenance.

reviews.rationale: The claim's main point, that key AGI ingredients are missing, rests on a 'might' premise and is stated as 'strongly suggesting'. Under the policy that is hedged, graded language and is not scored. Separately, e1 does support the firm sub-premise that LLMs were weak at planning in 2023.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assessment in his co-authored post. The definition it applies is his own.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the 'classical criteria' qualifier and 'hardly qualify'. Reading 'LLM's' as current LLMs fits the context.

contract.note: It uses Marcus's own definition and allows for ordinary human error, which is a fair, ordinary reading. The result depends on the threshold an evaluator picks for human-comparable reliability.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own March 2023 statement that GPT-4 is not fully reliable. This partly supports the reliability point, but it is the developer's statement about its own model and has no human comparison.
Microsoft's 2023 'Sparks of AGI' study reports human-level performance on many tasks. The authors' framing cannot stand in for measured reliability, so this qualifies the claim without settling it.

reviews.rationale: The packet has OpenAI's admission that GPT-4 is unreliable and evidence of broad capability, but no representative human-comparable evaluation covering flexibility, resourcefulness and reliability together. The contract needs that to decide the claim either way, so the evidence leaves it unresolved.
